etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English tyde, tide, tyd, tid, from Old English tīd (“time”), from Proto-Germanic *tīdiz (“time”), from Proto-Indo-European *déh₂itis (“time”), from Proto-Indo-European *deh₂y- (“to divide”). Related to time.

definitions.definition: The periodic change of the sea level, particularly when caused by the gravitational influence of the sun and the moon.

quote.citation: c. 1605–1608, William Shakespeare, “The Life of Tymon of Athens”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene iv], page 88, column 1:
quote.text: Go I charge thee, inuite them all, let in the tide / Of Knaues once more: my Cook and Ile provide.

definitions.definition: (chronology, obsolete, except in liturgy) Time, notably anniversary, period or season linked to an ecclesiastical feast.

quote.citation: 1590, Edmund Spenser, “Book I, Canto II”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London:  […]  [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC, stanza xxix:
quote.text: [...] and rest their weary limbs a tide.
Which, at th'appointed tyde, / Each one did make his Bryde

quote.citation: 1655, Thomas Fuller, The Church-history of Britain from the Birth of Jesus Christ until the year MDCXLVIII‎[1]:
quote.text: at the tide / Of Christ his birth

quote.citation: 1837, Thomas Carlyle, The French Revolution: A History […], volume (please specify |volume=I to III), London: Chapman and Hall, →OCLC, (please specify the book or page number):
quote.text: What is singular too, the spademen seem to work lazily; they will not work double-tides, even for offer of more wages, though their tide is but seven hours[.]

definitions.definition: (regional, archaic) A point or period of time identified or described by a qualifier (found in compounds).
Something which changes like the tides of the sea.
Tendency or direction of causes, influences, or events; course; current.

quote.citation: 1599 (first performance), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Iulius Cæsar”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene iii]:
quote.text: There is a tide in the affairs of men, / Which, taken at the flood, leads on to fortune [...]

quote.citation: 1622, Francis, Lord Verulam, Viscount St. Alban [i.e. Francis Bacon], The Historie of the Raigne of King Henry the Seventh, […], London:  […]  W[illiam] Stansby for Matthew Lownes, and William Barret, →OCLC:

definitions.definition: (transitive) To cause to float with the tide; to drive or carry with the tide or stream.

quote.citation: 1623, Owen Feltham, Resolves: Divine, Moral, Political:
quote.text: They are tided down the stream.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To pour a tide or flood.
(intransitive, nautical) To work into or out of a river or harbor by drifting with the tide and anchoring when it becomes adverse.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English tiden, tide, from Old English tīdan (“to happen”).

quote.citation: 1779, David Dalrymple, Annals of Scotland‎[2], volume II, page 121:
quote.text: I wit not what may tide us here
